title: So, can AI assess writing?
author: Daisy Christodoulou, Chris Wheadon
summary: No More Marking reports results from CJ Lightning, in which AI made Comparative Judgements on the writing of 5,251 Year 7 students alongside human teachers. The AI agreed with humans on 81 percent of 3,640 decisions, against 87 percent agreement between humans on a prior assessment. The authors argue the pattern of disagreement matters more than the headline rate, because older essay markers achieved good correlations while rewarding superficial features. Their review found the ten biggest disagreements were all human error, such as handwriting bias or misclicks. They add concurrent validity and standards-maintenance evidence and propose hybrid judging with 10 percent human input, while openly promoting the free summer projects.
points: AI agreed with human judges on 81 percent of decisions versus 87 percent human-human agreement, so the quality of disagreement is the real test.
Early essay markers got impressive correlations by judging length, so the risk is being right 80 percent of the time and wrong when it matters most.
The ten largest human-AI disagreements reviewed were all human errors, including handwriting bias and clicking the wrong button.
Asking an AI to make Comparative Judgements and validating them against human judgements gives assurance that a bare chatbot mark lacks.
Hybrid assessment with about 10 percent human judging validates the AI and keeps teachers engaged with student writing while cutting workload.
quotes: We now have results. Our headline finding is that AI is very good at judging student writing and is a viable and time-saving alternative for many forms of school assessment.

In total, our human judges made 3,640 decisions. Of these 3,640 decisions our AI agreed with 81% of them. On our most recent previous human-judged Year 7 assessment the human judges agreed with each other 87% of the time, which is fairly typical.

However, total levels of disagreement are not conclusive. The type of error matters. The overall agreement can be good, but if the 20% of disagreements are full of absolute howlers, that’s still a huge problem.

But their major weakness - and a major weakness of AI applications more generally - is that they could be “right 80% of the time, and wrong when it matters most”. It's possible for an AI system to get an impressive-looking 80% agreement with humans, but for it still to be making its decisions using very different values than humans, which then leads to a) big howlers in the 20% of disagreements and b) easy ways to game the system.

The famous example of this was a paper showing you could cheat an AI essay marker by writing the same paragraph 37 times. The cheating was rewarded because the AI essay marker was generating those impressive correlations by largely judging on length.
Our qualitative review of the ten biggest human-AI disagreements is that they were all some form of human error, not AI error.

Anyone can upload a set of essays to a chatbot and ask the chatbot to give the essays a mark or a grade. The problem you have then is - how do you know those marks or grades are right? How do you identify the ones that might be wrong without going through and remarking everything yourself?
